newsitem.title: USA: Minn. lawmakers open Twins stadium debate Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Minn. lawmakers open Twins stadium debate Thursday.

text.p: Minnesota lawmakers are scheduled to begin meetings this week on proposals to build a new ballpark for the Minnesota Twins.
The meetings scheduled for Thursday and Friday will extend beyond discussions on the American League ballclub's demands for a new stadium, however.
Lawmakers are scheduled to take testimony from Minnesota Vikings officials and the Metropolitan Sports Facilities Commission in addition to the Twins.
They have also placed the downtown St. Paul hockey arena financing plan on the agenda, a legislative aide said.

Lawmakers rejected numerous financing plans for a new $350 million to $400 million retractable roof stadium for the Twins during the last session, prompting Twins owner Carl Pohlad to announce plans to explore the possible sale and relocation of the team.
Pohlad said he would consider legislative solutions before the end of the 1997 baseball season, but would not wait for the 1998 legislative session to make a final decision.

The Twins lease at the Metrodome runs through the 2011 season, but includes an escape clause the team can exercise after the 1998 season if ticket sales are poor in relation to the rest of the league or the team loses money for three consecutive years.
Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson has supported building a new ballpark for the team and plans a special legislative session in September to consider a financing plan.
Legislative leaders named a bi-partisan 16-member task force to review the legislative proposals and take additional testimony before the upcoming session.
The Vikings and Twins have served as anchor tenants at the commission-owned Metrodome since it opened in the early 1980s.
The Vikings believe the discussions should be "all-inclusive," said Stewart Widdess, vice-president of marketing for the National Football League team.
"Before the Twins get an individual stadium, all sports franchises should be addressed and the community should be given the opportunity to decide what is right," Widdess said.
"Obviously, no one is going to risk the strong bond positions of the State of Minnesota or Minneapolis," Widdess said.
St. Paul officials have approved plans for a $130 million arena to house the new National Hockey League franchise for the city scheduled to begin play in the 2000-2001 season.
Carlson has pledged $65 million of bonds for the arena in the state bonding bill next year and St. Paul has approved backup financing if the pledge fails to materialize.
St. Paul has also committed to providing $30 million of bonds for the arena and the expansion franchise ownership group will provide $35 million.
